## Overview

Four ideas carry everything on this page:

1. **Resolution order.** A bare `image:` name resolves pin first, then the local cache, then the search path: `INSPECT_RANGES_REGISTRY`, an ordered comma-separated list whose default is the public catalog (`docker.io/meridianlabsai/inspect-ranges`). First match wins, and a broken location aborts resolution with the location named rather than silently falling through.

2. **Locations are interchangeable.** A location is the public hub org, a private OCI registry, or a plain directory in OCI image layout. Identity is content: every artifact verifies by digest wherever it lands, and nothing unverified lands under a consumable name.

3. **Sticky, then explicit.** Once a name resolves into the cache, builds keep using the cached artifact even as registries move on. Moving forward is a deliberate act: `images refresh`, regenerating a pin file, or consuming a republish (always a new digest; published bytes never change under a name silently).

4. **Specs travel by git, artifacts by registry.** A built range publishes under its spec's normalized-form hash, and eval init pulls the published build matching the cloned `range.yaml` exactly. That join is what makes clone-and-eval work.

[Distribution](distribution.qmd) is the mechanics reference behind all of this: the location grammar, verification semantics, and the full verb surface.

## The Catalog

The standard images publish at the project org, each consumable by bare name (hub repos are spelled `inspect-ranges-<name>`; specs keep writing the bare name):

| Name | Contents |
|---|---|
| `attack` | The standard attack box: a kali-class toolset (nmap, hydra, sqlmap, john, gobuster, impacket, metasploit, and more) built by a pinned recipe over the noble golden. `/etc/attack-image.manifest` records every delivered package and version, and the image refuses to build if anything listens beyond loopback. A dedicated attack box with no `image:` boots it by default. |
| `ubuntu-noble` / `ubuntu-focal` | Golden chains (image, provenance sidecar, vendor base), each with the guest control daemon baked in. |
| `daemon-bundle` | The guest control daemon artifact, for fleets that derive their own goldens: `daemon-bundle --pull` fetches it with no Go toolchain. |
| `inspect-ranges-range` | The hardened range container, published as a conventional Docker image and consumed by digest pin (below). |

The republish discipline: every consumer-held artifact is digest-verified, a republished image is a new digest, and the attack image's recipe version must bump for each republish, so the realized identity re-keys. Between publish days the catalog deliberately drifts from upstream feeds; the manifest records what shipped.

## Deployment Shapes

### Connected (the Default)

Nothing to configure. At the first eval, init pulls the published build and whatever catalog images are missing, digest-verified, with docker-pull-shaped progress; warm evals cost zero network. One operational caveat: anonymous hub pulls are rate-limited per address (measured 2026-10-18: 100 pulls per rolling hour), so a fleet cold-pulling the public org should mirror it or front it with its own registry (next two recipes).

### Mirror the Catalog

``` {.bash filename="Terminal"}
inspect-ranges mirror \
    --from docker.io/meridianlabsai/inspect-ranges \
    --to registry.example.net/ranges

export INSPECT_RANGES_REGISTRY=registry.example.net/ranges,\
docker.io/meridianlabsai/inspect-ranges
```

A mirrored root carries its transitive closure, so pulls work identically from the mirror; prepending your registry shadows catalog names deterministically, with the org as the fallback for anything not mirrored. One hub caveat: the hub does not expose org enumeration, so whole-org mirrors from it name their artifacts explicitly (a published catalog list is a recorded follow-up). Mechanics: [Distribution](distribution.qmd).

### Private Registry for Your Own Ranges

``` {.bash filename="Terminal"}
cd my-range/            # a built range
inspect-ranges push --to registry.example.net/ranges
```

`push` uploads the build manifest and its transitive closure (realized images, provenance, recipe bundles) and registers the exact-spec reference that eval init resolves. Consumers prepend the registry as above and run `git clone`, `inspect eval`. Pushing to the public org is the project publisher's job, never a user move.

### Air Gap

``` {.bash filename="Terminal"}
inspect-ranges mirror \
    --from docker.io/meridianlabsai/inspect-ranges \
    --to ./archive
tar -cf archive.tar archive/   # carry across the gap, untar
export INSPECT_RANGES_REGISTRY=/mnt/archive
```

The consuming session is then identical to a connected one, because identity is content, not transport. The daemon bundle travels with whole-location mirrors, so air-gapped fleets can derive their own goldens too.

### Pinned Fleet

``` {.bash filename="Terminal"}
inspect-ranges images pin \
    --from docker.io/meridianlabsai/inspect-ranges \
    --out pins.json
export INSPECT_RANGES_PIN_FILE=pins.json
```

A pinned host lands exactly the recorded root digests and refuses `pin-mismatch` when the first location serving a name no longer serves its pinned root (resolution aborts rather than falling through). Moving the fleet forward is the explicit act: `images refresh <name>`, or regenerating the pin file.

### Locked-Down Host

`INSPECT_RANGES_NEVER_PULL=1` pins a host against implicit transfers: the provider's auto-pull and the build's registry tier refuse or skip instead of touching the network. Explicit verbs still work, because typing them is the operator's intent; a fully offline host simply configures no reachable locations.

### Range Container Pin

The range container is an ordinary Docker image, so it distributes as one, and consuming the published image is a mandatory digest pin (a mutable tag could swap the hardened jail under a fleet):

``` {.bash filename="Terminal"}
export INSPECT_RANGES_RANGE_IMAGE=\
docker.io/meridianlabsai/inspect-ranges-range@sha256:ab12e0...
```

Unset (the default and the dev loop), `up` builds the image locally from package data. The pull is a plain `docker pull`, so hub credentials and private mirrors work as for any image; one caveat for hosts logged into the hub with a narrowly-scoped org token: docker sends the stored credential for public pulls too and the hub rejects an insufficiently-scoped token rather than falling back to anonymous, so public `docker pull`s fail on such a host (the distribution client is unaffected). Details: [Distribution](distribution.qmd#the-hardened-range-container-image).

### Self-Derived Goldens

Deriving your own goldens is the alternative to pulling the published ones: the fleet and air-gap path, and the only path for vendor images the catalog does not publish. It extends the digest chain back to the vendor image: `derive` pins the vendor image by digest and, given `--daemon-sha256` (the digest `daemon-bundle` printed at publish), pins the daemon artifact out of band too; without that flag the artifact is verified against its co-located sidecar only, which proves internal consistency, not provenance.

`inspect-ranges daemon-bundle -o <dir>` builds the guest control daemon artifact: a byte-deterministic tarball (static Go binary, installer, unit file) plus its `daemon.json` digest sidecar. It requires the pinned Go toolchain and is the only command that does (`--pull` fetches the published bundle instead, needing no toolchain); built artifacts are consumed everywhere else by digest, so one publish serves every host. Publish to the shared artifact cache (`~/.cache/inspect-ranges/artifacts`) and `images derive` finds it by default. The publish output ends with the bundle digest; record it and pass it to `derive --daemon-sha256`. A missing or wrong-version toolchain refuses with the pin named; builds are reproducible, so an unchanged source tree yields the identical bundle digest.

`images derive <vendor-image> --sha256 <digest>` produces a daemon-baked golden overlay in the image cache: the vendor digest verifies before anything is written, the daemon artifact verifies against its sidecar, the daemon and its unit are baked, ssh and every stub listener are disabled, and a provenance sidecar records all input digests. Failure modes, each stage-named: vendor digest mismatch (nothing written); missing, tampered, pin-mismatched, or protocol-skewed daemon artifact (each error names the `daemon-bundle` republish command); an unmanaged file squatting on the target name (never clobbered); a corrupt provenance sidecar; interrupted derives (self-healing on the next run). Re-running with the same inputs is a cache hit that re-verifies the recorded digests. Ubuntu noble vendor images are the Linux scope; Windows goldens derive locally with `images derive-windows` from user-supplied evaluation media (install ISO + virtio-win ISO, both sha256-pinned) and are never published; the Windows examples' READMEs ([goad-light](https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/inspect_ranges/tree/main/examples/goad-light), [splunk-detection](https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/inspect_ranges/tree/main/examples/attack-range-windows)) cover the specifics.

`images list` shows managed goldens with provenance, build-captured realized images (flagging superseded generations no manifest references), and everything else: unmanaged files, stale derivation and capture temps, goldens whose recipe version is behind, and legacy double-suffix names. `images prune` reclaims what no manifest references; it reports by default, deletes with `--yes`, and refuses while registered projects exist unless forced (build success already prunes its own range's garbage, keeping one previous generation for rollback).
